description: A passionate solo participant interested in space exploration, science and technology. I aim to develop an innovative solution to a NASA challenge using research, creativity, and programming. I look forward to learning continuously new skills and creating a meaningful project that addresses a real-world problem.
summary: Space Heritage Explorer is an interactive website that tells the stories of equipment humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars, built for the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” Visitors rotate 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, click a pin at each landing site, and read the object’s purpose, location, status, last contact and story. We cover 11 objects, from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 11 descent stage to Viking, Spirit, Opportunity and the Ingenuity helicopter. A “Start the story” walkthrough steps through the hardware in order of arrival, and a lifespan chart shows how long each object operated, from arrival to last contact. Visitors can also search by name, mission or site, share a link to any object, and open NASA’s image library for photos. It is built with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so it loads fast, works on any device, and supports keyboard use. These objects are the first archaeology beyond Earth, and telling their stories builds public appreciation for exploration history and for protecting these sites.
details:
What it does
Space Heritage Explorer is an interactive website that tells the stories of equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Visitors drag a 3D globe of each world, click a pin at a landing site, and read the object’s purpose, site, agency, arrival year, last contact and story. We cover 11 objects: 4 on the Moon and 7 on Mars. They range from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 11 descent stage to the Viking landers, Spirit, Opportunity and the Ingenuity helicopter. A “Start the story” walkthrough steps through the hardware in order of arrival, and a lifespan chart shows how long each object operated, from arrival to last contact. Visitors can search by name, mission or site, share a link to any object, and open NASA’s image library for more photos.

Benefits and intended impact
These objects are the first archaeology beyond Earth. The site makes that history easy to explore for students, teachers and space fans, and it builds public appreciation for exploration history and for protecting these sites. Showing lifespans side by side also makes the engineering stories clear, such as Spirit and Opportunity far outlasting their planned 90-day missions.

Tools and technology
Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks or libraries. The globes and star field are drawn on the HTML canvas. Mission facts come from NASA mission pages, and photos come from NASA’s image library, including images from the Lunar and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiters. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages.

What makes it creative
Instead of a list of facts, visitors fly across the Moon and Mars and discover each object where it was left. The story mode turns the hardware into a timeline of exploration, from the first landings to the last signals. Mars and the Moon each have their own colors and surface look, which gives each world its own feel.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard controls for the globe and story navigation, readable contrast, and reduced-motion support.
  • Performance and reach: no build step or dependencies, so it loads fast and works on phones and laptops.
  • Accuracy and credit: facts based on NASA sources, with NASA and the mission teams credited for imagery. Landing-site coordinates are approximate.
  • Inclusion: both NASA and Soviet missions, to tell the full story of what humans have left behind.
